skill.name: The topic sentence that guides a paragraph
skill.why: A topic sentence tells you what the whole paragraph is about.
skill.how: Find the sentence that every other sentence backs up. Check each one fits.

beats.say: A paragraph is a group of sentences about one idea.
The first sentence often tells you that idea.
beats.show: **Mo's cooking is dangerous.** His toast set off three alarms.

beats.say: That's the topic sentence. It's the boss of the paragraph.
Every other sentence backs the boss up.
beats.show: Mo's cooking is dangerous. **His toast set off three alarms.**

beats.say: If a sentence doesn't back up the boss, it doesn't belong.

encounters.text: ___ A sea anemone looks like a plant, but it is really an animal with dozens of stinging tentacles. Most small fish keep well away, because one touch can stun them. encounters.frame: Gus is writing a paragraph about stomachs. The Heddrake swallowed his topic sentence.
encounters.text: ___ The acid inside your stomach is strong enough to dissolve some kinds of metal, so you might expect it to eat through the stomach itself. It doesn't, because the stomach has several clever defences. Its inside wall is coated with a thick layer of slimy mucus, which stops the acid from touching the stomach's cells. The cells in that wall also release a chemical that weakens any acid that gets too close. This mucus is constantly topped up, so there is never a gap for the acid to sneak through. Some of the cells that make the acid even sit tucked away in tiny pits, out of its reach. Even so, some cells do get damaged, so the stomach replaces its entire lining every few days. Its muscles keep squeezing and churning, mixing food with the acid while keeping the wall moving. Thanks to all of this, the acid breaks down your lunch without ever breaking down you.

encounters.text: ___ After an earthquake, rescuers must find survivors inside collapsed buildings that could crumble further at any moment. Instead of sending people in first, many teams now send snake-like robots that can wriggle through gaps narrower than a person's arm, carrying cameras, microphones and lights. During bushfires, drones fly through thick smoke that would blind a pilot, using heat cameras to spot people and animals that are trapped. After an accident at a nuclear power station in Japan, robots were sent into areas where the radiation was strong enough to make a person seriously ill within minutes. Police use tough, tank-like robots to inspect suspicious packages, so that no officer has to stand beside one. Underwater robots check bridges and ships for damage after storms, so divers don't have to search in dangerous currents. Some robots can even carry water bottles and radios to trapped survivors while human teams dig towards them. In every case, a person still steers the robot, watches its cameras and decides what to do next, but that person can stay at a safe distance. Each robot that goes in first means one fewer human life put at risk.

parts: . A top speedrunner might repeat a single tricky jump hundreds of times in one evening, alone in their room, until their thumbs move without thinking. Many record every attempt and then watch the recordings back frame by frame, looking for the exact moment where they lost a fraction of a second. They break a game into short sections and drill each one separately. Then they practise joining the sections together. Most attempts still end in failure, so they reset and try again. Before a serious run, they write out a route, listing every shortcut, every enemy to skip and every item to grab, and then they memorise it like a script. Some spend months on a single game, playing the same opening level over and over until their timing is perfect. Even after a record, they keep practising, because someone else is always practising too. When a world record finally falls, it is almost always because someone has put in more hours than anybody before them. As one record holder put it, the fastest run looks effortless only because of the thousands of slow ones behind it.

encounters.frame: The Architect wrote a paragraph for the Tower Six hut, where everyone says there's a ghost. The Heddrake has the topic sentence.
encounters.text: ___ Some buildings produce very low sounds, from wind rushing past or old pipes rumbling, that are too deep for our ears to hear. Experiments have shown that these sounds can still make people feel uneasy, shivery or as if someone is watching them. Old timber floors creak and pop as they cool down at night, which can sound remarkably like slow footsteps in an empty room. Draughts sneaking through cracks in walls can create sudden cold spots and make doors swing open on their own. Certain moulds that grow in damp, closed-up houses have been linked to headaches and confusion, which can make people doubt what they are seeing. Our brains are also wired to find faces everywhere, so a stain on a wall or a curtain in the moonlight can look alarmingly like a figure. Tiredness plays a part as well, because a sleepy brain is far more likely to mistake a shadow for a person. Even suggestion matters: people who are told a house is haunted report many more strange experiences inside it. Bad air from old heaters can also cause dizziness and strange visions, which is why investigators often check for it first. None of this proves that ghosts don't exist, but it does mean that a creaky, chilly house is not good evidence that they do.
encounters.prompt: Which topic sentence fits this paragraph best?
encounters.success: Low sounds, cooling floors, draughts, mould and face-spotting are all ordinary causes of 'ghostly' feelings.

options.text: Ghost stories have been told around campfires for thousands of years.
options.reason: The paragraph never mentions the history of ghost stories. It explains spooky feelings.

options.text: Many so-called hauntings have simple scientific explanations.
Sounds too low for us to hear can make people feel uneasy.
options.reason: That's only the first detail. The paragraph gives many other explanations too.

options.text: Scientists have now proven that some old houses really are haunted.
options.reason: The paragraph says a creaky house is 'not good evidence' for ghosts. Nothing is proven.

encounters.frame: Wren wrote a paragraph about snow gums for the Architect. The Heddrake has the pieces of her topic sentence.
encounters.text: ___ In winter, the high country around Scaffold Peaks can drop to fifteen degrees below zero, and snow can bury the lower branches for months. Snow gums cope by making a natural antifreeze in their leaves, so the water inside doesn't turn to ice and burst the cells. Their leaves are thick and waxy, which stops them drying out in the icy air. Their branches are bendy rather than stiff, which lets heavy snow slide off instead of snapping them. Summer brings a different danger, because the same slopes can be swept by bushfires. A fierce fire may burn every leaf on a snow gum, but a woody lump at the base of its trunk, protected by the soil, survives the heat. The lump is packed with stored food and sleeping buds, ready for exactly this moment. Within weeks of the fire, that lump sends up bright green shoots, and in a few years a new ring of trunks has grown. Some snow gums on the slopes have lived through several fires this way over hundreds of years. Many other trees would be killed outright by a fire that strong. That is why so many snow gums on the peaks have several twisted trunks instead of one.
encounters.prompt: Build a topic sentence that covers the whole paragraph.
encounters.success: The first half is about freezing winters and the second half is about bushfires. The topic sentence covers both.

accept: Snow gums can survive both freezing winters and fierce bushfires.
body.reason: Half the paragraph is about winter cold and half is about bushfire. Wind isn't in it, and they do survive.
